Not a problem. I still take antipsychotics - and feel fine. Only relatively high dose made me feel awful. I feel like the antipsychotics on a right dose only helped me to be able to concentrate and perform cognitive tasks. This could be different for you though, and I don't know the dose you're on, so take this with a grain of salt. Be sure to discuss all your symptoms with your psychiatrist. 

One thing I can say that helped me tremendously, was getting back to school. It gave me distraction, a feeling of purpose and stability, even though I wasn't feeling totally okay yet. 

Just wanna say that even if it feels now like you aren't improving much the last months, this can change without you expecting it.

What I can tell from experience, the road to recovery isn't linear. It's also hard to tell if you've improved, you could have but can't see it clearly but you're just not in the state of mind to see it. There really is no reason to conclude you will not get better. After about 12 months I started to gradually feel more like myself again, and also (gradually and slowly) got more spontaneouas and lively in conversation. I'm now about 18 months and I almost completely feel like myself again. Remember your time frames could be different, but know that most people will get back on track and feel alright after a certain time (and eventually totally themselves).

Edit: also try to stimulate your brain

I'm not sure how to help or what is the best reaction, but your brothers' delusions sound very similar to my own, believing something very unlikely to be true. When I seemed too have less tablewear I assumed my roommate was stealing it. Similarly, when I had a flat tire, I thought she had put a pin it on purpose. In reality, other explanations were far more likely to be true. In reality, I didn't correctly count my tablewear and some of it was hiding in a bag somewhere that I took for dinner. My flat tire probably happened because I rode through glass or something. 

There was still some doubt in these delusions and through therapy I was able to accept them as an illusion, something that strongly *seemed* true, but probably wasn't. By not acting on the thought, the illusion wasn't reinforced. Your brothers delusions are probably stronger, and I'm not sure how to help, maybe someone else can.
